la:adj:sonorus.html:
sŏnōrus, a, um (collat. form sŏnōris, e, and 498), adj.
sonor
,
noisy, loud, sounding, resounding, sonorous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for the class. sonans): cithara,: aes,: arcus,: tempestates sonoras,: tonitru,: pelage, Lachm.: flumina,: nemus,: Phocis (on account of the Delphic oracle),: insula fluctibus,: versus qui crepitant pronuntiatione fragosā et exsultantem informant dictionem, ut (): at tuba terribilem, etc., P.—* Adv.: sŏnōrē, loudly: oscitavit (with clare),.

la:verb:sono.gloss: to sound, resound, make a sound or noise (and various sounds in-context)
senses: to sound, resound, make a sound or noise (and various sounds in-context)
to sound, utter, speak, express, call
to cry out, call; sing; celebrate, praise, extol
la:verb:sono.html:
sŏno, ŭi, ĭtum, 1 (ante-class. collat. form acc. to the 3d conj., sonit, Enn. and Att. ap. ; sonunt, Enn. and ; Enn. ap. P.;
inf. sonĕre, Att. ap. ; ; part. fut. sonaturum, ; perf. sonaverint, ; gen. plur. sonantum, ), v. n. and a. [Sanscr. svan-, to sound; cf. O. H. Germ. svana; Engl. swan].
Neutr., to make a noise, to sound, resound: aes sonit, the trumpet sounds, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 213 Vahl.): plectra, tympana, * et saep.: cujanam vox prope me sonat?; ; ; : hic mare sonat,; cf.: mare, silvae Aquilone,: omne sonabat arbustum fremitu silvaï

frondosaï, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 196 Vahl.): clamore viri, stridore rudentes,: omnia passim mulierum puerorumque ... ploratibus, et saep.: (hirundo) circum Stagna sonat,; cf. : saeva sonare Verbera,: classica sonant,: displosa sonat vesica,: fletus rixaeque sonant,: natura fert, ut extrema ex alterā parte graviter, ex alterā autem acute sonent,: dicta non sonant, do not chink (i. e. are not money), .—Impers. pass.: jubet tibias agere: sonatur,.—

Act., to sound, utter, give utterance to, speak, call, cry out, sing, pour forth (syn.: edo, eloquor, cano): homines inconditis vocibus inchoatum quiddam et confusum sonantes,uttering, pronouncing,: sonare subagreste quiddam,to speak,: pingue quiddam,; cf.: (Sibylla) nec mortale sonans,: illa sonat raucum,; cf.: nec vox hominem sonat,does not sound like that of a human being,: tale sonat populus,calls, cries out,: exululatque Evoeque sonat,; 4, 523: atavos et avorum antiqua sonans Nomina, boasting of, vaunting (syn.: crepans, jactans),; cf.: sonant te voce minores,: ut haec duo (honestas et utilitas) verbo inter se discrepare, re unum sonare videantur, to signify (syn.: significare, indicare),; cf.: quā deterius nec Ille sonat,: Epicurum non intellegere interdum, quid sonet haec vox voluptatis, id est, quae res huic voci subiciatur,: furem sonuere juvenci,i. e. they betrayed him by their lowings,Pythius in longā carmina veste sonat,sings, pours forth, accompanies on the lyre, (3, 29), 16; cf.: sonante mixtum tibiis carmen lyra,: te sonantem ... dura fugae mala,: te carmina nostra sonabunt, shall sing of, i. e. shall celebrate, praise, extol, ; so, Germanas acies, Daca proelia,: acta viri laudesque,.— Pass.: sive mendaci lyrā Voles sonari,; cf.: magno nobis ore sonandus eris,.—Hence, sŏ-nans, antis, P. a., noisy, sounding, sonorous (very rare): meatus animae gravior et sonantior,: quod est sonantius et elatius,.

la:noun:sonitus.html:
sŏnĭtus, ūs (
gen. soniti, Pac. and Cae cil. ap. ), m.
id.
, a noise, sound, din, etc. (class.; in sing. and plur.): at tuba terribili sonitu taratantara dixit, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 452 Vahl.); cf.: lituus sonitus effudit acutos, id. ap. Paul. ex Müll. (Ann. v. 522 Vahl.): summo sonitu quatit ungula terram, id. ap. (Ann. v. 281 Vahl.); imitated by Virg. A. 8, 596: ungularum,: tumultuosus,; cf. : forum,; ; : armorum,; : vocis,: tubae,: tubarum,: ventorum,: remorum,: pedum,: convivarum,: stertentium,: Olympi,i. e. the thunder,: (ignis) ingentem caelo sonitum dedit,: utero sonitum quater arma dedere,; : sonitum (veneni e poculo ejecti) reddere,: fragor et sonitus,: verborum sonitus inanis,—Plur.: nosti jam in hac materiā sonitus nostros,i. e. my thundering speech,; innumeros aeris sonitus,: sonituum discrimina,; .— Of an abstract subject: quae (eloquentia) cursu magno sonituque ferretur,.

la:other:Sonus.html:
sŏnus, i (collat. form sŏnus, ūs, in
gen., ; abl. sonu, Sisenn. ap. ; ; nom. plur., ), m.
sono
, a noise, sound (syn. fragor): et pereunte viro raucum sonus aere cucurrit, Enn. ap. Lact. ap. (Ann. v. 509 Vahl.): tympana raucis Obstrepuere sonis,: non exaudito tubae sono,: signorum sonus,; cf.: cum ingenti sono fluminis,: olli respondit suavis sonus Egeriai, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 122 Vahl.): tantus et tam dulcis sonus,: distinctus,: ab acutissimo sono usque ad gravissimum sonum,from the highest treble to the lowest bass,: in tibiarum cantibus varietas sonorum,: (lingua) sonos vocis distinctos efficit,: ad nervorum eliciendos sonos,; : inpulit aures Confusae sonus urbis,; ; ; : inanes sonos fundere,to utter empty sounds, Kühn.—
Fig., tone, character, style: et in tragoediā comicum vitiosum est, et in comoediā turpe tragicum, et in ceteris suus est cuique certus sonus,: unus enim sonus est totius orationis,; .—
Of language, sonorousness: gravitas et cothurnus et sonus Sophocli,.

la:adj:sonipes.html:
sŏnĭ-pēs (sŏnŭpēs), pĕdis, adj.
sonus
,
with sounding feet, noisy-footed (poet.): turba (in Isidis sacris),.—As subst., noisy-foot, i. e. a horse, a prancer, steed: fremit aequore toto Insultans sonipes et pressis pugnat habenis,; ; ; ; (in Cic., sonipedes is cited as an example of a fourth pæon, de Or. 3, 47, 183).

la:adj:sons.html:
sons, sontis, adj. (
nom. sing., ; ) [Part. from root as-, es-; Sanscr. as-mi; Gr. εὶμί; Lat. esum, sum; cf. Gr. ἐτεός, ἐτήτυμος; prop. he who was it, the real person, the guilty one].
Guilty, criminal; subst., a guilty person, an offender, malefactor, criminal (freq. and class., esp. as subst.; syn.: reus, nocens): anima,; : ulni,: di,: manus foedata sanguine sonti (poet. for sontis), : morae ab igne supremo,.—Subst.: sontes condemnant reos, * : (minores magistratus) vincla sontium servanto,: punire sontes,: insontes, sicuti sontes,: manes Virginiae nullo relicto sonte tandem quieverunt,; ; ; ; ; .—Gen. plur.: sontum,.—
Hurtful, noxious, acc. to (but no example is preserved).—
Neutr. sing., sin, offence (eccl. Lat.), .
